What an experience!

Comparing it to Left 4 Dead or Back 4 Blood are not comparisons without merit, but being VR, the immersion is brought to a whole new level.
And the VR aspect is done extraordinarily well, and in a fashion that will suit just about every VR user!

For example, when it comes to motion, you can use teleport movement ala Half Life Alyx, or you can use regular movement via the toggles. Both have their drawbacks and positives, both suit different players.

The firearm handling is fantastic for a game like this, and again, is designed to suit all players.
You can use your off hand to steady a weapon, even one handed weapons such as pistols, or duel wield pistols, or use consumables ect.
Weapons have weight, recoil is noticeable and reloading has been handled perfectly. There are two settings, manual and easy.
Easy is where, to reload you just bring bring your firearm to the ammo on your rig and bam, magically reload your weapon - in the same vein as a lot of wave shooters.
Or you can manually reload your firearm - eject the magazine, push in a new one, rack the slide ect. As a bonus for taking the harder route and extra steps of manual, you gain a 35% damage increase to balance it out against easy reloading, which is just fantastic and opens the game to everyone.
Again, with weapon storage, you can choose to have holsters like in Saints and Sinners, or you can go for a traditional gaming weapon select wheel.

TLDR: The devs have really taken the time to make After the Fall as approachable as possible for every type of VR gamer, whether they come from Pavlov, Half-Life, Saints and Sinners or obscure wave defence games.
Firearms are fun to use, they have weight, oomph, recoil and can be operated realistically or not.

Graphics are pretty nice! If it was a PC title, not so much, but in VR they look fantastic and are very atmospheric. 

There are a large number of unlocks, a hub area, you can play solo with bots or group up with friends or strangers to tackle different difficulties or even game modes.

I don't (yet) have the playtime to declare this a must play title for VR gamers, but I'm close to doing so.

L4D on VR, with some mild roguelike elements to keep things fresh.

Really digging it so far. The aesthetic feels like Division 1 meets Dead Space, with a dash of 80s cyberpunk. Satisfying, familiar VR gunplay that you can set to either reload arcade-style like Arizona Sunshine, or have the realistic reloading of games like Pavlov (which grants a bonus to the currency you earn.) 

At launch there are only six weapons and five levels to play. Weapons all have unlockable cosmetics and upgrades that you'll find randomly during your harvest runs. Weapon performance can be very heavily affected by these, so it's possible to construct very different feeling guns from the same archetype in the game's weapon bench. 

Upsides: 
-Gunplay and weapon upgrading is fun and interesting, if a bit RNG for me.
-Interesting level design for VR. There are some ziplines that make me wish I had something to shoot while sliding
-Ammo boxes are fun to slap
-80s arcade theme and soundtrack are great
-Matchmaking with crossplay between steamvr, oculus, and PSVR is nice for playerbase
-Intuitive and simple (in a good way) inventory system. I never felt bogged down by it in combat, but swapping items can be a little tricky sometimes.
-Rewards scale with difficulty, so the best stuff will take some real skill to acquire.

Downsides: 
-Not a lot of content at launch, but planned seasonal updates from what I've read should remedy this
-Enemy variety is pretty limited right now. There are only a handful of special enemies. 
-Somewhat janky reloads due to ammo pouch placement. I have to choose between having holsters in a good spot or ammo, and it would be nice if the two could be adjusted separately.
-Juggernaut arms are throat-seeking grappling hooks that will hit you at weird angles if you try to juke the Jug

Wishlist:
Obviously more guns, enemies, and stages are the big ones
Some kind of endless mode or horde defense to break things up

Overall, I could see myself dumping another 20 or so hours into it in its current state, especially with friends. You can really feel the Arizona Sunshine roots here, but I do think they could use a little more dynamism with enemy spawning. That said, the gunplay feels good and rewards reload skill and shot placement. I've never had an easier time dual wielding in VR.

Great game as a shoot and loot, the weapon options are generalized, like there's only one "low caliber" pistol, one shotgun, etc. The weapons handle well and they aren't ridiculously difficult to find. The storage options are definitely a con. For instance, from what I can, tell you can only carry two weapons (any in the game really) on your hips, that's it. and as far as gadget/consumables storage, think Half Life: Alex but with just the wrist storage. This is a minor inconvinience if youre finding collectables but still need a syringe or an explosive so you have to make sacrifices and for that i consider it an added awareness that the developers purposely included to kind of encourage players to play as a team. I can respect that. There is another con, probably the most annoying but it could be just me. When you're either trying to pick up [insert any item here] you almost always accidentally grab an item that is on you instead of the item that you're reaching for on a ground, table or even in a drawer. For example: I find a syringe to heal myself because I play like a tank, the game will either force whatever is on my wrist in my hand, or one of my weapons from my belt...that aren't any where close to my hands. It's not game-breaking but it definitely is frustrating.
As far as combat is concerned, the shooting is very fluid, like if you're a good shot the game is actually playable and the enemies actually die.  The optional reload mechanics are really useful and rewarding if you choose the advanced option (realistic-ish reloading) which is an extra 35% damage if you choose this option. 

Missions do get kind of repetitive but I only had time to play four or five of the first missions and they all seem to have the same objective pattern: shoot deadites, get to safe house, shoot deadites again, get to safe house again, fight a big guy, you win, groovy.  All in all this game is very good, at this point in time, with the current available content, i'm not sure if it is $40.00 great. With that being said I haven't played the game or story all the way through so this review is just a potential buyer review and if you ask me, I recommend After The Fall.

Whether you're a VR veteran or just strapping on your headset for the first time, After the Fall offers a heart-pounding, action-packed experience that’ll leave you shouting, “One more round!” So, gather your team and take on the cold, because survival is a dish best served ice-cold. 🧊🔥

After The Fall is a polished, engaging arcade shooter that moves faster than anything else available thus making it a refreshing experience that never gets tiresome in contrast to other titles that are slow and tedious to the point where they become plainly boring.

Online play is surprisingly stable and solid - it looks they've surely taken the time to craft a good network environment for the players to engage. I've never been kicked out during play though I've read other players who did. In that regard, maybe those people did not possess a good connection to start with. Either way, it's only going to get better with time.

The central gameplay of After the Fall is to hastily work your way through a level, taking on hordes of monsters, stopping off at occasional safe houses, collect as much Harvest as possible from dead enemies while featuring a good dose of exploration during the times spent inside buildings to find key items that will improve your arsenal.

The graphics, in the highest settings, are quite beautiful with the various objects and environments being well designed and rendered. The models carry much detail, the textures are clean and crisp, the shadows blend smoothly and the overall look of the game feels very polished and gorgeous.

To sum it all up, Vertigo's latest creation manages to combine all the good elements present in other VR games but at the core, it remains a fast, unrelenting, arcade shooter with a neck-breaking pace as its main card.

This game blew me away! I was going into this expecting Left 4 Dead in VR and not much else (which isn't a bad thing) but there's just so many more mechanics on top of the base game to keep it fresh with a lot of replay value.

If you'd like to see gameplay you can skip into my video https://youtu.be/X56JKuSyASw

Basically you replay levels to find secrets, get money and unlock new weapons / weapon mods. 
There's shops in the middle of levels that you can buy items at, or avoid spending to earn the most money possible (which is SUPER RISKY on harder difficulties).
There's also a cool mechanic where a less experienced VR player might prefer to reload their gun by sliding it over the ammo belt, but if you're used to physically reloading, you gain extra money from kills by doing so. The game is littered with fun little features like this!

After the Fall is also completely crossplay, which is amazing! I was playing with someone on Oculus and PSVR while I was on Steam. The game uses it's own in-game friend codes and the lobby allows tons of players at once, so you can always find someone to play with or just let matchmaking find someone automatically (there is an option to play with bots too if you want).

One thing I want to point out: Access the settings / options by pressing in the right Joystick (on Valve Index, not sure on other controllers). That's how you can change snap turning, sprint settings and stuff.

This game has a few issues but nothing that can't be fixed.

First off, having such large interaction zones makes this game harder than it needs to be. Too many times will you try to grab your gun with your off hand and end up grabbing a mag off your chest, or worse when you try to grab a holstered gun and you jedi an empty bottle off the ground instead.

Next issue is the gun system. Guns feel alright to shoot but I have no idea why to this very day devs keep setting your grab as your weapon manipulation bind.

PLEASE FOR THE LOVE OF GOD SET TRIGGER TO GUN MANIPULATION OR ADD AN OPTION TO. 

I'll try to use my off hand to support my 1911 and end up grabbing the slide even when the slide is farther from that hand than the grip was. Mix that with the ammo being on your chest and large interaction zones and its a gamble whether you grab the guns grip, slide, or another mag out of your pouch.

I'd highly recommend adding options for play styles like Pavlov or Onward when it comes to how ammo and gun interaction is handled.

As for graphics and performance graphics is good, not amazing but good and modern. 

Performance on the other hand seems to need some work. The game seems to crash if you are using alot of RAM even if you have 20GB more to spare and even with a 2080ti and 9900k frame rates aren't what I was expecting even at low settings. I had to use fholger's scaling .DLL and tinkered to get a good balance.

That said I do recommend this game, its fun if a bit less intense than others and cross platform play is a real show stealer.

I've been playing this game quite a lot on the PS5 and loved it, so I thought I would get the PC version and see what it looks like with the graphics cranked up - good is the answer, although, to be fair, the PS5 version is sweet.

The gunplay is smooth and fun once you get the muscle memory working for you. The environments are well laid out and beautiful, and the various corridors and arenas have been planned with fun horde defence in mind. You can feel the pedigree of Arizona Sunshine 'shining' through in this title.

I have played in co-op mode a couple of times and have played loads in solo. The AI team members are OK on the whole, they do sometimes get in the way, but this is rare and momentary. 

The premise is quite simple, you are a runner and go on various 'runs'. On your way through each run you collect goodies, if you complete the run, you get all of the goodies, if you die, you lose the items but keep the money. The money and guns can be upgraded, broken down or scrapped. For example, if you find a gun with an ammo counter, collect the gun then strip it down when you're back at the hub.

All of this gives a great deal of replayability. The various difficulty levels don't just nerf your guns. They directly alter the feel of each run. Hordes will be larger and more aggressive, and health will be sparse to non-existent, but with this, the rewards are greater. 

I love this game and Arizona Sunshine, the balance between gun realism and fun gameplay is excellent.

A Fun left 4 dead style shooter for VR
I never thought I would see the day where I would see Left 4 Dead in VR.

[h1] Basically VR's first L4D [/h1] 
Cool game with significantly higher production quality compared to other similar games of this type (the co-op zombie slaying kind) - and this game is focused on fun (i.e. action and combat) over realism (which is severely lacking in the VR industry), i.e. it's not a survival game just like how L4D was never about survival and resource management - meaning no need to worry about durability, hunger, etc. 

[b] Bugs [/b]
There ARE a couple of game breaking bugs however, and the most significant one is the presence of ghost lobbies/hosts that prevent players from jumping into a game - you can't choose to explicitly 'host' a game; if the game netcode determines that someone has started a party for the same mission before you, you are forced to join them instead, and since you can only 'actually start' (i.e. load into) a mission if you are host, you'll never be able to play because the dead host is dead and won't let the party load into the mission, ever. 

Anyways that's all I have to say for bugs.
Onto the good stuff!

[b] Great focus on action and combat over cookie-cutter 'realism' and 'survival' [/b]
No 'durability'.
No 'hunger'.
No 'fatigue'.
Just lots of action and gun combat against hordes of zombies. 
The only thing you have to 'manage' between games are your gun upgrades (sight, stock, grip, magazine, etc.). 

This is [i]exactly[/i] why I like this game a lot - because it's simply not focused on 'realism' at all, which almost every other VR game of this type irritatingly seems to be obsessed about, specifically with regards to resource management - in this game you have tons of zombies to shoot, and fittingly, you therefore require lots of ammo, which the game does provide in abundance. 

Restocking ammo isn't a chore, meaning more shooting and less fumbling. (this alone puts this at the top of my personal list of 'VR co-op zombie slaying' games)

[b] Ammo/item pickup design [/b]
There are L4D-esque ammo stashes that appear at multiple points throughout each segment of a mission - you need only touch the ammo cache or shoot it once to restock on all types of ammo - no need to manually reach over and pick them up individually, magazine by magazine, like in other games. 

The game also borrows HL:Alyx's convenient method of picking up items in-game - when you're in (close) proximity of an item, the game allows you to hover your hand in its direction and grab to pull the item to you from a distance, except in this game the item doesn't 'fly' towards you, it just teleports into your hand. 

They also have the same the wrist pouch storage concept that Alyx had, and there's nothing wrong with copying a good concept from another game - if anything, this is good, because it encourages the better VR interaction design patterns to become the standard rather than the exception, i.e. more VR game devs need to adopt this type of interaction. 

[b] For physical VR gunstock users [/b] 
This game works extremely well with a gunstock, but only for the two handed weapons (obviously), and there's only two of them in the game.. and both are assault rifles. 
There's also the pump shotgun.. but you don't use a gunstock with that for obvious reasons. 

After a lot of trial and error, I found that these are the most optimal settings for use with a VR gunstock: 
[list]
[*]MOVEMENT > Control Scheme: Sliding (i.e. continuous locomotion - if you get motion sick don't use this)
[*]MOVEMENT > Sprinting mode: [b]Muzzle sprint[/b] (same as pavlov where you autosprint when gun barrel is pointed down)
[*]GAMEPLAY > Inventory Mode: Selection Wheel*
[*]GAMEPLAY > Reload Type: Quick**
[*]GAMEPLAY > Grip Mode: [b]Toggle[/b]
[*]GAMEPLAY > Hand Item Swap: OFF
[*]GAMEPLAY > Weapon Weight: OFF
[/list]
[i]*'Selection wheel' inventory mode uses HL: Alyx's method of switching weapons, but if you prefer VR immersion, use the other one ..I think it's called the 'belt/holster' option - basically your weapons are shown physically on your hip and you grab it to swap your weapon. Personally I don't like using this anymore because of the amount of fumbling that occurs when you're trying to swap your weapon or grab an item that's also overlapping with where your hip weapon is etc. The other reason to use selection wheel mode is because of the ease of usage with minimal hand movements needed to swap weapons[/i]

[i]**'Advanced reloading' is cool and immersive but at higher difficulties the quick reload makes a world of a difference, and not worth the extra harvest bonus that it gives - just remember that you can collect partially used magazines which gets discarded when you do a tactical reload (i.e. you reload with a few bullets still available in mag). You can do this for both types of reload modes[/i]

Note that bolded options are the critical ones, while the non-bolded options above are just my personal preference, and is additionally also subject to whether you like your experience to be 'realistic/immersive' or not. However, regardless of your preference, this specific configuration will minimize fumbling outside of combat, thereby maximizing your time spent in combat (which is what the game is about, really).

Left 4 dead 2 but in vr

Simply, it is what it looks like: a left4dead inspired zombie shooter. There are a few 'specialty' Snowbreed as well as run of the mill Common, and you and your team are part of a network of harvesters that farm them all like caddle.

The variety between 'campaigns' (5 at launch) is somewhat appealing, with a slightly different way to traverse the landscape of the level in each, however the frozen/snowy theme of the games universe makes many rooms look the same after some time playing, and there is not much variety at all in terms of 'finale' events (except the last mission, which even then is only marginally different). In left 4 dead, for each campaign you play, you are in essentially a totally different enviornment than the others, with a clear goal set out since you first load in and different enviornmental obstacles you must overcome. There were flooded neighborhoods turned into swamps, abandoned carnivals and festivals, a giant mall with different shops that leads to the highway, and other ways that the enviornment itself plays a large part in how the level is played. As you're playing you are getting closer to that specific goal, and preparing yourself accordingly, perhaps with different strategies for different scenarios. In ATF, every level feels the same in that you are only there to harvest the resources of the snowbreed, passing through frozen rooms of frozen buildings with the same few frozen desks scattered about, and the absolute only goal you have is to survive the really, really big wave at the end :o!
New harvest runs in the future must do something to stand out from the rest, or I feel much of the community will get bored of the game quickly.

Gunplay is satisfying, with enemies reacting appropriately to being shot in different parts of the body, and satisfying sound effects and visuals like gore to make popping zombie heads feel that much better. Weapons have considerable recoil, but this can be lessened by attachments you unlock as you play, and is still managable regardless (no randomized spread, simulated physical recoil of the gun)

The attachments are worth elaborating on as well, as this is the main differing factor in the comparison to left 4 dead. There are six guns in the game, a 9mm pistol as well as desert eagle, an uzi inspired smg, a generic assault rifle, an ak-47 style rifle, and a pump shotgun. You unlock each as you progress through the different harvest runs for the first time, or you can also find one early during a run. The attachments, however, are randomly unlocked by finding floppy disc items during a run and surviving. Harder difficulties give better chances of spawning high tier floppys. The guns themselves and the attachments are paid for with the harvest you collect in runs, and up to six customized guns can be stored to swap loadouts between runs.

Overall, I think the game is fun to play. It feel gud to shot gun in vr. However, there are some bugs at launch that I have to wonder how they could have gone unnoticed or launched with, like owned guns or attachments disappearing. There is also definitely something left to be desired in terms of making each level different in an engaging way, or giving the game just that little bit more depth and personality that left 4 dead had instead of essentially killing the zombies for sport. I think that is what made left 4 dead such a memorable game to so many people, by somehow providing a more immersive experience with the characters on a personal level and the world they live in on a flat screen than this game does in VR. There is a cast of 4 playable characters in this game, and I couldnt tell you any of their names except Jimmy since he seems the last to be filled when loading or if down a player. There's no mention of them at all in the 'story' you're given, they just feel like random, faceless, personality less bodies filling the job. Still, the game is enjoyable and easily replayable, I just hope for good things to come in the form of additional content.

Oh, there's also pvp, if you're into that. I haven't tried it yet as I find myself loading other games to play for pvp.

2) Even though it's called 'Launch Edition', it more feels like Early Access edition. There are some confusing controls that sometimes just don't register grabs or momentum at the right time (I.E. Index controllers grabbing objects far away from your hands instead of ones you're touching, instantly teleporting off cliffs in walking mode [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2711700798]WHICH CAN END YOUR MISSION BTW[/url], life-saving and/or unlockable items getting stuck in FRICKING CABINETS UGHsahjdf). I'd really like a chest to store my weapons instead of having to rebuy them and upgrade them all over again whenever I wanna swap weapons. My gosh. Gosh the attachment system gets me so grumpy.

At least the glitches are hilarious! T-posing enemies charging at you, flying beasts you can't shoot because they're behind an invisible wall, bouncing foes if you get a headshot on them whilst they're mid-scripted animation.... mwah, magnifique. Maybe cute cosmetics or a way to spend it to have a higher chance of getting unlockable attachments that I'm just not lucky enough to get!

This game is still ridiculously unique in the VR market (for now lol) but your mileage will very depending on how you feel about games that request you grind like you have no life and that you play the same single digit number of missions over and over again. Interested in the story so far. I do wish there was a bit more of it strung together but this isn't a story heavy genre so I'll take what I can get.

The NPC dialogs are interesting but I hope they don't get repetitive. We heard about the old mans date back to back on Chinatown. If I hear that dialog every single run, it's really going to grate on my nerves. That being said, the voice acting is really good. There's some lip flap that doesn't quite line up if you're looking for it but it's far from a major issue.

Visually the game is amazing. Comparable or better to Alyx. There's a nice variety of enemy appearances and as we saw at the end, higher difficulties offer even more variants. I believe I've seen 3 special zombie types at the moment and they're certainly miniboss title worthy opponents. Especially the grabber police a--hole. The Smasher makes for a great boss while also getting hounded by hoards of other Snowies. Environments felt large and lived in. Felt like we were really in the midst of some post apocalyptic town. I loved the mix of interior and exterior environments. My one concern here is that there are only 5 maps atm if I remember correctly. That could get repetitive quick but I expect it will take a decent number of hours to work up through 4 difficulty levels across all 5 maps. At about an hour per run, that's 20 hours to hit all maps on all difficulties. Well worth the price IMO. You'll also more than likely need to grind a little bit for gear or floppies and no one is going to play a perfect no failure game so that 20 is a minimum.

The available comfort options and options across the board are exceptional. Very happy to see this becoming more standard with AAA titles. The one critique here is that I don't think the game ever told you how to open the menu. I randomly discovered it. In a social game it seems very necessary to show the player how to invite and accept invites from players.

Speaking of players I loved the lobby. Everyone was silenced which was golden, but you could see others running around and going about their business. It was an unexpected and nice touch.

The crafting system is neat. Doesn't seem very deep but I like the ability to customize and dangling loot in front of my face will almost always work...

I have very little in the way of negatives to bring up about the game that aren't just potential fears about content or incredibly trivial. Population isn't a concern as the AI isn't terrible. This is what I expect from an experienced VR dev. Great work guys. 100% recommended. Pick this up ASAP. This is going to be a blast with a group of friends.

Easily one of the best VR games around with a few QoL Issues

[b]Good[/b]
[list]
[*]Shooting is satisfying and each weapon has its own recoil and feel. 
[*]Enemies are a bit slow to compensate for a VR playstyle, but ignoring them will cause you to quickly get swarmed
[*]Bigger enemies/bosses will break your teams formation and cause you to work together and changes the pace
[*]There a decent amount of upgrades to earn through gameplay
[*]Good weapon variety
[*] Challenge really ramps up on harder difficulties 
[*] Cool 80's-ish retro aesthetic with the Arcade machines
[/list]

[b]Could use some work [/b]
[list]
[*]Shotgun feels a bit wonky since you have to pump a new shell and you have to really pump far and can feel disjointed
[*]Using manual reload feels a bit unintuitive (will elaborate down below) and not worth the extra in-game currency for upgrades/power-ups
[*]Personal complaint but some sections are a bit dark and looking around gets kind of disorienting
[*]There is a small reward for exploration, but not enough to make it worth the time
[/list]

[b] Manual Reload [/b]

Manual reloading requires these steps and it gets really complicated especially when you're trying to not die in the harder difficulties:
[list]
[*]Ejecting your magazine with a button
[*]Grabbing another from your chest which never feels properly aligned
[*]Putting another magazine in
[*]Chamber another bullet - this has caused me to smack my controller together on more than one occasion and doesnt feel right like in other games like Pavlov
[/list]

Using the quick reload option simply requires you to eject the magazine and put the gun near your chest/ammo pouch which is less finicky.

I'm not sure what the fix for this is, and it's not the biggest issue because you always have the option for the easier reload method, but its a huge part of the game and while I want the extra harvest (upgrade currency) its not worth getting my cheeks clapped.

Conclusion: Great experience that's worth everyone's time if they like co-op Left 4 Dead style shooters. Cross-play is the icing on the cake. If the Devs continues to update QoL issues and produce content, it could be one of the greatest VR games.

After the Fall: Surviving the Apocalypse with More Zombies and Less “Help” Than You Expected

Alright, so you thought the zombie apocalypse would be all “Let’s grab some guns and save the world,” but let’s be honest After the Fall isn’t about saving anyone. It’s about surviving. And by surviving, I mean barely making it through with half your squad screaming for help, while the other half gets eaten by terrifying mutant zombies that have somehow figured out how to jump, climb, and apparently take over your nightmares.

The game is a co-op survival horror experience, so it's basically Left 4 Dead but on steroids. But not the "healthy muscle growth" kind. More like the “What the heck did I just take and why is everything trying to eat me?” kind.

The Zombies: First things first these zombies aren’t just “shuffling around with a ‘boo’” kind of guys. These mutants have agendas, and they do crossfit. The standard zombie will lunge at you like it's trying to get a spot on the Hunger Games roster. Then you’ve got the big ones. The ones that look like they’ve been to a few too many protein shakes and now they’re really mad. You’ll spend a solid chunk of the game just running for your life, thinking, “I’m just here for the loot, please don’t eat me.” You’ll feel like you’re in a horror movie that’s been directed by an ADHD-suffering octopus.

And when you think you've dealt with one wave of grotesque, hungry mutants, another wave comes rushing at you faster than you can say “I regret everything." The game loves to remind you that you're never truly safe. Oh, you killed that boss zombie? Great. Here's another one. Enjoy.

The Horror: You know that feeling when you’re playing a game and everything is going okay, and then suddenly you hear a weird noise, and you stop breathing because you’re convinced that something’s about to jump out at you? Yeah, After the Fall does that. A lot. Like, you’ll be walking down a seemingly quiet street, thinking everything’s fine, and then BOOM a screaming mutant is suddenly right in your face. And you scream too, but with way less grace and way more "Please God, don’t let me die" energy.

The tension is deliciously horrifying. One minute, you’re casually reloading, and the next, you’re panicking because your teammate got grabbed by some hideous beast while you're too busy trying to remember how to shoot. It’s a constant struggle between fear, adrenaline, and the realization that your survival instincts are trash.

Co-op Chaos: But here’s the kicker you’re not alone. No, no. You’ve got friends. Or at least, that’s what you tell yourself until one of them gets caught in the middle of a zombie horde and decides to scream like it’s the end of the world. Which, to be fair, it is.

Co-op play is where the magic happens. It’s you and your team, fighting for your lives against impossible odds, which quickly devolves into a series of panicked moments where everyone yells, "OVER HERE! HELP! NO, NOT THAT WAY, THE OTHER WAY!" Meanwhile, half the team is dead, and the other half is definitely questioning why they agreed to play this in the first place.

The Weapons: Okay, let’s talk weapons. They’re fun. They’re amazing. They’re satisfying. And when you’re holding that shotgun and blasting zombie after zombie, it feels like you’re a bad-ass. But and this is important the moment you miss, you start thinking, “Maybe I should’ve gone with a crossbow. Maybe I can just sneak by…” Spoiler: You can’t. You will be swarmed. You will be overwhelmed. You will be screaming for your friends to save you, only to be answered with the sound of death as they get eaten alive.

The Story: You’re trying to survive in a post-apocalyptic world full of mutants, with some story about fighting back against the apocalypse and maybe, just maybe, saving humanity. It’s not exactly Shakespeare, but who needs a deep plot when you’re busy surviving wave after wave of mutants that seem to have no concept of personal space?

Final Thoughts: After the Fall is a constant rollercoaster of horror, chaos, and humor mostly because you’ll laugh hysterically when your friend gets caught in a zombie pile-up while trying to reload. It's the perfect game for people who want to survive the apocalypse, but also enjoy the occasional “OH GOD, WHY DID I SIGN UP FOR THIS?” moment. The zombies are relentless, the environment is creepy, and your chances of survival are slim especially if you're playing with people who think running toward danger is a good idea. But hey, that’s what friends are for, right?

So grab your gear, trust no one (except maybe your real friends), and dive into a world where every corner could hide a mutant, and every shadow might just be your death sentence. Welcome to the apocalypse, my friend. It’s loud, it’s terrifying, and it’s a heck of a lot of fun.

After The Fall is a really fun VR CO-OP Multiplayer shooter (there is a PVP mode but it isn't the main focus of the game). I'd say this is a good game but not a great game. The main thing to know is the core game play loop is fun, getting kills is satisfying, teamwork pays off, and the novelty of something being like L4D in VR is nice to have.

[i]So to put it simply, all my issues with the game don't come from the core game play but rather lack of what could be.[/i]

The issues I have are the lack of variety in the special infected and lack of maps.
Before I go out on a limb here, I just want to say I have hope that the game will be updated and hopefully most of my problems will be fixed but as of 12/11/21 these are my opinions.

The lack of maps isn't a huge issue currently but once I get into that ~24 hr mark I'm probably going to be wanting more from this game. The levels are replayable to some degree and getting kills is satisfying but a reason why I and so many others keep coming back to L4D is the fact that it has community made content and a plethora of maps. I'm not saying this game will get community made content nor do I think there will ever be support, but its wishful thinking to have hope for a tool set that would allow such.  Therefore, having only a few maps is definitely going to get stale pretty quickly.

Next, the lack of variety in the special infected makes runs underwhelming. The current roster of what they have is fine but c'mon, we neeeeeed moooooore! To add insult to injury, there are two special infected who do nearly the same thing, there is a brute who is a tanky MF with a whole lot of health. Then, there is a charger like thing that can run pretty fast and also tank quite a few bullets. Then there is the eater who is similar to a boomer, but that is it. More special infected designed around VR interaction would be really awesome and definitely spice up the game play, especially since a whole lot of stuff in this game is just shoot shoot shoot. 

In conclusion, After The Fall is a game that is fun, but if not updated to add more content and variety, will probably sit up on the old retired steam games library shelf after hitting that ~50 hr expiration date. I am enjoying myself at the time and I have faith in Vertigo to be able to update the game to extend its replayability beyond its current capacity.

After the fall is a fun vr wave shooter game. It revolves around you entering these harvesting sites, clearing them for harvest which is just the currency for the game and then returning back to hub. You just clear an area, head to another area and clear that until you get to the end which usually has a boss or a really big wave from what I experienced.

The reward for completing harvest runs is obviously the harvest currency which you spend on attachments/new guns and equipment in harvest runs. The other reward would be attachments for your guns. This is somewhat annoying as you can get dupes of weapons which means you need to do runs quite a bit and it doesn't show what quality the attachments are so its a shot in the dark until you get the first couple.

Attachments changes the way the gun looks slightly and there are weapon skins which are obtained by doing challenges with that specific gun. Either clearing out hordes of mobs or landing a certain amount of head shots in a row so if your into that then this game has that.

The downside of this game is simply the fact you will at least need one other player to complete maps. The bots are terrible. They are good for clearing out the hordes but once it comes to the boss fight which every maps have then its entirely up to you to solo it. If you haven't have much experience with the boss then you would end up going down as the boss has a one shot move which will kill you if your don't run until it finishes it. This took a while to learn and even then its hard to pull off as your most likely the last one alive and any mistakes will end the run. Even if you aren't, the bots will go down soon enough and if you were to go down then you get to witness them just stare at the boss while shooting then die.

Now the other downside is that it takes a while to find one other player. Sometimes you get lucky and somebody joins instantly and get to go or your just sitting in the lobby waiting for somebody. Maybe you just get somebody that joins then instantly leave. It would've been fine if the bots are somewhat manageable but knowing that I am just gambling on the 20% of the time everything works out that it just gets frustrating. Also there's a chance you have a bad connection to them or the other way around so they all could disconnect at the end which is sad as they miss out on the rewards. Had that happen once and had multiple disconnects from hosts other times.

A small nitpick is that the boss for the instant kill move doesn't make any noises so if your looking away for a moment and miss it then you'll usually end up dead. It's usually fine if its just the boss but usually the game throws the boss in with a wave ongoing so it gets hectic at times. Its manageable with players but bots...expect 2 or more dead by the time the wave is dead and the boss is left.

Overall its a fun game with players but terrible if your expecting to go through the game alone with bots on veteran difficulty. All of the players I met that had voice chat enabled are pretty nice and chill on the north america server.

--------------------------------------------------

[b]PROS:[/b]

-4 Player co-op VR shooter

-Weapon customization is great!

-Weapons feel good, Landing headshots is fun

-Does offer exciting gameplay in bursts

-After getting accustomed to the game mechanics, I would say it has good controls (confusing to learn though)

-You have 2 holster slots to store weapons, but you can essentially carry 4 weapons in total, as weapons and items in your hands are retained. (I carry a rifle, SMG, and akimbo pistols into each run)

-Enemy spawns have *some* variety; Bosses always appear in same areas, but hordes are somewhat variable.

-Lots of control / movement settings available (though the game doesn't explain what some of them really do)

-Manual reloading (realistic) or auto-reloading options available to players

-Game has a Multiplayer HUB area and Party system (party invites, friend invites, etc...), though it is far from perfect as I detail in the CONS section

-Has PVP mode

------------------------------------------------

[b]CONS:[/b]

-Game is short and lacking for content. 5 levels; 4 difficulty settings; 6 weapons; 2 items (pipe bomb + healing syringe); 3 types of elite enemies; 1 Boss enemy. If you make a point to run through all 5 missions before replaying any, you will see 90% of what this game has to offer in your first 2-3 hours.

-Game's Party / Lobby system is under-baked. If returning to the HUB area, it always disbands your party. Lack of player communication options (as outlined below this) compound the issues with this strange party system.

-Lack of voice/text chat in HUB areas. Technically voice chat exists, but if you aren't in the same HUB instance with your Party (which you can't do anything about), you can't hear each other until you enter the match. Accepting a Party invite does not load players into the same HUB Lobby. Too many times I have queued Quick Play matchmaking, got placed into a full Party, and sat waiting 5+ minutes for the seemingly-AFK host to start the match, with no way to communicate with them. I've started Reporting AFK hosts, as at least the game offers this option and 3 out of 4 Quick Play parties I join result in this issue.

-The shotgun is powerful but really suffers from VR-reloading woes if using manual reloading. It's really easy to do in the firing range, but under pressure, reloading the shotgun really isn't an option if you are trying to prevent taking damage.

-Game completely neglects to inform the player of so many mechanics. Weapon storage in the firing range. How to swap items between hands. How to even bring up the Settings menu. Informing the player that having an item in your off-hand doesn't prevent you from manually reloading (aka you don't need to drop a pistol when dual-wielding to complete a manual reload). NPC gives you a wrist-mounted rocket launcher, but doesn't tell you what it is or how to actually use it.

-Allies controlled by AI constantly strafe in front of your shots

-Big progression issues; after beating all 5 levels, the only progression that exists is collecting weapon parts. Compared to the time it takes to complete all 5 missions (1-2 hours), you will experience many hurdles trying to grind for weapon parts that have any value, as outlined below.

[b][u]ISSUES WITH FLOPPY DISKS / UNLOCKING WEAPON PARTS:[/u][/b]

1. Unlocking new weapon parts is achieved by finding hidden floppy disks in missions (color-coded to indicate rarity) and inserting them into machines in the mission's 2 available Safe Rooms, rewarding the entire party with an unlock at the end of the mission. If a floppy is found in the last 3rd of a mission, only the player carrying the floppy disk is rewarded as the final Safe Room has nowhere to insert the disk. Imagine the party is rewarded with 2 of the lowest quality floppy's, and 1 player finds a high-level floppy near the end and only they get to profit from it.

2. Duplicate parts can be acquired. The closer you get to finishing your favorite weapon, the greater the chances of getting duplicates.

3. Since the parts you get are totally RNG, you may get 10 parts for a pistol you don't use before you get any parts for the weapons you actually use.

We had to get organized calling out wave spawns and specials and rationing scavenged supplies; pick the right difficulty and you will be getting an active co-op experience, not a shooting gallery where your friends are only there for moral support.

Although there aren't many missions there is an extensive crafting and progression system. If you play for completionism's sake there might be a few months of content in there alone. Guns have unlockable achievement skins (i.e. flame decals on the deagle require a 100 accurate shot streak) and also attachments that significantly change their behavior: extended magazines, reflex sights, grip tape, and even special mods like batteries that add crit chance. I've barely scratched the surface but pimping your favorite gun or unlocking a new toy seems like the main reason to load back in.

A few more thoughts:
If you're having trouble with manual reloads go to game settings and change "grip type" to "manual" OR turn off hand swapping.

So far I'm not impressed with the specials, especially compared to L4D or Back 4 Blood. For the most part they're just slightly different bullet sponges. Classic enemies like the Witch would have been incredible in VR, or lickers from Resident Evil (even the normal snowies will climb on ceilings).

Performance is definitely playable 60+fps w/ Quest 2 on a rtx 2080 over airlink 5ghz. As part of the PC master race we're getting dramatically improved visuals compared to the Quest & PSVR players. I'm still hoping there are small performance improvements with patches though. 

We'll see if people are still playing it weeks from now but as it stands I think it's easily worth full price. This is the new benchmark for VR co-op.

After the Fall executes its vision of Left 4 Dead in VR with gusto, as it brings much of what made Valve's four-player co-op great back 2008.

 There's still room for improvement when it comes to enemy variation and object interaction, but fans of arcade shooters may have a hard time knocking it on this alone, as it competently brings PC, PSVR, and Quest 2 in one big cross-platform splatter fest.

This should be at the top of co op PVE VR titles. It has its issues, but whatever issues existed at launch, I have yet to experience. The Multiplayer works extremely well, along with in game voice chat. The graphics are not HLA quality, but still at the top compared to 90% of VR titles. You will have the odd time that reloading a mag (if you have manual reload enabled) will not go and sometimes need to drop the mag and grab another one. This happening is rare though. Its also more demanding of your GPU compared to Arizona Sunshine imo. However, dropping graphics to low to accommodate, doesn't change the visual quality all that much. Still above 90% of pcvr titles out there imo. 

My largest gripe is the story is weak. It exists for 3/4 of the maps. I'm assuming the maps with zero story are the ones that were added later. So its basically a looter shooter. I usually don't enjoy any game without a good story, but for some reason this one just works. Wish more VR players would pick this up. Very satisfying gunplay. 

Damn the devs for abandoning it. I mean, thanks for Sunshine Remake and part 2 (which wasn't THAT good), but I mean here, there is a system for a lot of replayability. Same idea could be added to Arizona Sunshine (yes I know horde mode exists but that's a very niche audience). 

Either way, buy this game. It goes on a great sale sometimes. And honestly even full price is half of what a decent or worse Meta Quest games cost.

Hands down the best Co-op VR experience I've ever played. 

Pros:
- Graphics on PC are great. Not as good as Half Life: Alyx, but they come close.
- Runs great. I haven't experienced any performance issues, even when 30+ zombies are on screen at one time.
- Tons of replay value. The different XP levels feel balanced and fair, and require higher levels of coordination to beat each difficulty.
- Cross-play & Cross-buy (for Quest) are a great features that you don't see for many VR games. I really hope this trend continues since it lets me play with more of my friends.
- A super friendly and helpful community. The majority of players use their mics, and everyone I've met so far was more than willing to teach new players. I've put in over 50 hours now and I haven't ran into A SINGLE SCREECHER.


Cons:
- Some game-breaking bugs do exist. Vertigo Games seems to be patching most of these out quickly, but I ran into one last night when a player got locked in the safe room right before the final boss.
- Difficulty levels aren't locked, so brand new players who haven't even beaten the game can jump into Nightmare and ruin the run for everyone else. In my opinion players should have to at least beat all maps on Veteran before they can do Master runs, and beat all maps on Master before they can start playing Nightmare.
- Needs more content. Within 10 hours you'll have seen everything the game has to offer, barring some weapon skins and attachments. 
- Players can't rejoin the run if they leave. This is a big issue right now since game-breaking bugs force many players to leave, which can ruin the run for everyone.

[h1]This is Left 4 Dead or Back 4 Blood in VR[/h1]

I whole heartily recommend this game for those who want a Left 4 Dead or Back 4 Blood in VR, because this is it. After the Fall is an awesome coop FPS experience. The gameplay is very action-packed, the graphics are actually very detailed, the sound effects are great, and the music is very 80s synth which really adds to the flavor of the environments. Although, this game is quite short (currently only 6 maps), but they are designed in a way to keep you replaying them. You also have challenges per each weapon you find/purchase that unlock different skins, and different attachments for the weapon. Also, the developers have vowed to continue to support the game for years to come which means more maps, game-mods, weapons, etc. in the future.

Very cool 4 player fast paced action game, the gunplay is very satisfying. It has realistic reloading on the guns (or arcady if you're into that) and guns upgrades and mods. The gun upgrading is done manually at a work bench which is pretty cool. Graphics look pretty cool too

Can be a little grindy since parts after each run can be a duplicate which will be converted to harvest (in game currency). But overall this is a game to play in VR especially if you have a full party in higher difficulties.

After The Fall has been an enjoyable VR experience. It is pretty much your typical zombie shooter game with small 20-30 minute levels to complete for simple unlocks and general fun. The game has a good amount of replayability, relying mostly on the player's desire get better and increase their mastery of the mechanics. It does have some light random-reward/lootbox-like mechanics that I'm not [i]super[/i] fond of but it's not an intrusive skinner box system so I'll give it a pass.

The gameplay is pretty solid with a 4-player, co-op, PvE, repayable cycle. Gunplay is satisfying with two modes; simple and advanced. Simple allows you to just slap your guns against your chest to reload while advanced requires clip and bullet count management and, nicely, gives a small but measurable reward for going the harder route (beyond just being more fun). The game does technically have a PvP arena but it feels more like a novelty or 'something to do' once or twice more than any significant part of the game.

Difficulty ramps up pretty smoothly with the four levels of difficulty; starting with small numbers of slow, unarmored zombies and gradually increases to hoards of ice-shielded sprinting, murder monsters. Team play feels good when you get a group of people who work together and scraping out a win is very satisfying. Sound design is pretty good, guns are punchy without being overwhelming, the soundtrack is effective and sound effects round out the experience quite nicely.

The game is far from perfect, however, as the game has a host of bugs that range from mildly annoying to [i]how did this ship[/i]. To their credit, Vertigo Games did release this title simultaneously on all the VR platforms at the same time and they are still updating and supporting the game with regular fixes and content but having $60k of guns disappear off your hips randomly can very easily turn an enjoyable evening of zombie slaying into a sour ragefest real fast.
	
The game is best played with friends. While you can play with random people online, the skill level of individuals is extremely variable. You can get good games PUGing but you are more likely to find yourself stuck in a group of cheaters glitching through walls or AFKers or dealing with the host's (party leader's) spotty connection causing terrible rubberbanding while trying to get headshots.

Overall it’s a very fun game. At time of review, I have 70 hours in the game with the first major content patch 'Frostrunner' right around the corner and am looking forward to it.

There is basically 3 types of zombies being just a normal zombie, armored (higher difficulty, tanks more shots in certain locations), and crawling. After every mission you get money and blueprints. Money too spend on attachments/guns. There is a few different raritys so theres always a grind for better items. Blueprints can contain from guns, muzzles, grips, sights, and 2 different special modifiers. It creates a really fun and simple gameplay loop that helps encourage you too switch between weapons since you get upgrades for anything. Any weapon is viable as they all are balanced.

Theres a mutation gamemode that the zombies get special effects (always full armor, always crawling, etc) and instead of blueprints you get special modifiers for guns. (full auto, more damage, etc). Hopes were high based on Vertigo's track record with Arizona Sunshine, and they definitely did not disappoint. I finally get the KF2/L4D2 style horde shooter experience that I always wanted in a VR title.

Yes, I have my complaints and criticisms, but the devs are very open about this through the game's Discord channel, and that's all that really matters to me. These issues pale in comparison to the scope of this project, and the fact that no other developer has even floated the idea of making this type of game, let alone one that spans all major VR platforms, with the potential for cinematic and downright heart-pounding moments.

After streaming early access footage for viewers through our podcast, those who were viewing, particularly friends who formerly played KF2 with me, were immediately sold. It's clear that we now have something  that's here to scratch that itch.

WIth this being newly released, it's clear that Vertigo has a long way to go, especially when it comes to content. But with support and constructive criticism/feedback, After The Fall has the high potential to become a fun and memorable VR title.

You'll observe that I'm recommending this game but the entire rest of the review will be gripes. It's L4D in VR. There are no other coop VR games of any note, so it sort of wins by default. Basic gameplay is solid and other people elevate the experience. If you like coop, play AtF. It's as simple as that.

That said, there is so much wrong with this game. It is an absolute buggy mess. Weapons reset, weapon skins have weird resetting issues as well, progress can sometimes randomly halt, older players can't buy ammo for the awesome wrist rockets (but new players can), you can end up failing to join parties, which forces everyone in parties to wait several minutes for the game to figure it out. If someone does manage to join late, they join into a locked room so the mission can't be won unless they quit. All of the default settings are terrible (defaults to hand-orientation for movement, defaults 180 degree turns on--and the setting will reset to default every time you boot the game--defaults to snap-turn, and so on). Even the positioning of the magazine when you're loading pistols is bizarre. You can sometimes fall through levels and get stuck in a white void from which there is no escape, and you regularly get stuck in scenery which blacks out the screen unhelpfully and leaves you vulnerable but unable to move or shoot. There is currently a glitch allowing players to be unable to lose any run and zombies commit suicide if they can't path to players (which is part of how the glitch works), so all endgame play is just boring slow-paced auto-win glitching rather than exciting difficult gameplay. I've started a few times in the hub world instead of the match that just started, which again needs to be quit. Speaking of quitting, if you DO disconnect from host when launching into a match, you can't actually click OK on the popup, so you need to kill the game and relaunch it. Index players are uniquely unable to use a control scheme that allows 4 weapons instead of 2, easier multi-gun reloading, easier item pickups, and easier wrist rocket usage. The Index scheme is more immersive, but it isn't fair that Index gets forced to have an objectively harder game if they don't want to. Graphics were clearly made to be easily downgraded for the Quest 2 and so look very dated, but the game is a beast to run well despite that. And all of this is sidestepping the issue that the game has only 5 short levels and you'll see every single enemy in the very first level. For a game predicated on replayability, there is almost no content here. The first L4D had something like three times as many maps. And speaking of L4D maps, L4D had branching paths, many small rooms to search, and wide open areas with long draw distances at times. AtF simply doesn't. There is never more than one route forward and there aren't even that many side rooms/paths, nor does it ever seem to open up as much as L4D did. Nor does it have more complex encounters than "kill all the zombies". Never need to carry or interact with objects. No filling generator gas tanks one fuel can at a time, no shoving boards over to lay a bridge, or anything. Nor does AtF even have as many interactibles as Arizona Sunshine, their previous zombie game. That game had hats, pencils, staplers, books, coffee cups, just junk lying everywhere to fiddle with and you'd loot ammo from glove boxes, car trunks, etc. In AtF, everything comes pre-looted so there is almost nothing in the dead world. If a shelf of drawers has ANY drawers at all, those drawers WILL have items, so there's never the prospect of rifling through things. And those drawers don't tend to be very meaningful because ammo comes in giant brightly-colored crates that you shoot or smack for ammo for all weapons (except wrist rockets). It would have been more immersive and survival-ish if we had to properly loot apartments and vehicles (whose doors and trunks can be opened but which are ALWAYS totally empty) for the materials we needed to finish the run or the floppies that unlock weapon mods. Speaking of weapon mods, they are random chance, but that means it can be a nightmare grind to get the mods you direly need to play at higher levels. I have more playtime than 99.8% of players and I haven't unlocked the critical extended mags for either of my mainstay weapons. I have so much harvest (the game's currency) that it's been utterly pointless for dozens of hours, but harvest can't be used to unlock anything besides a selection of weapon skins. Also, though the game was sold with player skins, there is currently no way to apply the skins.

Despite all that, I've played a lot, because I enjoy gaming with friends and the basic gameplay loop is fun, when nothing gets in the way of it too much.

"The game, as it appears, is a zombie shooter that draws inspiration from the roots of Left for Dead. While it doesn't quite capture the same captivating essence as LFD, it manages to shine in several ways, keeping players engaged for a substantial amount of time. To be honest, I've spent more time playing this game than LFD, which indicates that the developers must be doing something right.

ATF offers a wide array of weapons and attachments, allowing players to customize their arsenal. Additionally, it provides a variety of useful items such as Health Stims, which can send gameplay into a thrilling berserk mode, intensifying the action by 150%. The inclusion of Pipe Bombs adds excitement, particularly for those special moments when you want to unleash a small tactical nuke on hordes of zombies. Moreover, each player receives a special gadget for each wrist, such as the mini-rocket launcher or the sonic sound device for close-range combat.

Initially, the game had a limited number of levels and activities to enjoy. However, over time, the developers have added a good selection of new areas to explore and battle in. Despite the game's strengths, there are a few downsides worth mentioning. Performance on Quest Link/Virtual Desktop can be an issue, as there seems to be some lag or micro-stuttering when moving your hands. This problem could be resolved by incorporating the Oculus SDK runtime, similar to the Oculus Store version. Personally, I own both versions, but I prefer playing on the Oculus version due to the lack of lag. Rather play on the Steam Version since I like it being in my steam library. Another drawback is the AI, which can be quite unintelligent. Although the developers have been attempting to improve the AI of the Jimmy character, they haven't quite succeeded yet.

In conclusion, this game is a highly enjoyable experience with significant potential for improvement. However, it's uncertain whether the developers will continue updating this title, as they are currently working on a sequel to their other cooperative zombie shooter, Arizona Sunshine."

After the fall does everything it says on the package. It's a *fun* zombie shooter. The story is nice (even though there's only about 10 hours max so far) the AI is great and the maps are detailed. I haven't run into any game breaking bugs, and only a few small annoying ones, like how holding your gun in your off hand makes it hard to grab ammo with advanced reloading. Aside from that, the controls feel great. I haven't played public lobbies because there's not many australian players, but I have played with a friend and it's been fun. 

Pros:
-The story. There's not much story content right now, but the game could just have easily given you no narrative and people would still enjoy it. As someone who enjoys playing for objectives, it's a pleasant addition.
-The AI. It's good, there's not much to say. They'll heal eachother and revive after a wave, and sometimes they even manage to save you in a tight spot. The voice acting is fun, and I admit that though sometimes corny, their interactions are funny.
-A great game with friends. Disclaimer, I've not played in public lobbies so I can't speak to them, but with friends over vc the gameplay is intense and enjoyable.
-Graphics and level design. This game looks GOOD. There's so much detail packed into every map. Even rooms you can't access have assets and aren't just blacked out. You can shine your torch through windows and boards and fuck dude it's just so pretty as someone who appreciates details like that. 
-Horde mode. Once you're done with the maps, or don't feel like committing to as much gameplay, horde mode is a great codzombies-esque wave shooter. I recommend playing with friends though, as there's no AI and solo can get hard. 

Cons:
-Controls. Overall, I do like the controls in after the fall, but there's a few bugs that can make advanced reloading frustrating and some of the weapons feel just about unusable to me. Though especially in your off hand, even playing with my right I found the shotgun annoying to pump and some of the dual handed weapons hard to cock. I love the smg and the pistol, but they're also just about all the guns I can play. Also, you just about *have* to play with the laser (and I recommend changing the colour from the default red, because it's quite hard to see), because the iron sights aren't too accurate. 
-Content. This one is a bit nit-picky, but there's not much content in the game currently. You get pretty much all of the guns playing the story content (10 hours *max* on your first playthrough), the last few maps have no objectives and as someone who can't play the pvp content, that, well, sucks. Skins are a fun little extra, but they feel like meaningless grind when you can't see yourself most of the time and weapon skins are client sided.

TL:DR
-Buy the game on sale, I don't think there's 45 dollars worth of content right now.
-Don't be afraid to use simple reload, or play easier difficulties to save yourself frustration. 
-Play with friends! (But if you can't, the AI is good too.) 

Overall, I'm having fun with this game so far. I recommend it, and I look forward to seeing it develop.

After The Fall delivers a distinct take on the cooperative VR shooter formula by plunging players into a frozen, alternate-1980s Los Angeles overrun by mutated creatures known as Snowbreed. Rather than leaning on the usual sun-bleached apocalypse aesthetic, the game wraps its ruined world in ice, snow, and biting winds, creating a uniquely harsh atmosphere that immediately sets it apart. The backdrop of abandoned malls, skeletal high-rises, and buried streets adds a chilling sense of isolation even when playing with a full squad. From the first mission onward, the hostile setting works in tandem with the action to create a constant feeling of tension: every echo, every distant roar, and every frozen alleyway reminds you that survival here is earned through grit and coordination.

The gunplay and physical interaction are at the heart of what makes After The Fall compelling. Weapons feel substantial and responsive, rewarding players who enjoy the tactile rhythm of VR shooters—slamming a magazine into place, racking a slide, or dual-wielding against an onrushing horde feels satisfyingly grounded. Each firearm has its own personality, and upgrading them over time adds a sense of progression that keeps missions engaging. The game strikes a good balance between arcade-style accessibility and immersive realism; it never becomes overly complex, but it still demands enough physical involvement to make firefights feel thrilling and high-stakes. Facing a charging Snowbreed brute or a swarm erupting from the ice becomes a chaotic, sweaty moment where instinct mixes with muscle memory.

The cooperative design elevates the experience further. Missions are built around four-player squads, and the game’s difficulty scales in a way that makes teamwork essential. Reviving fallen allies, managing ammo under pressure, and coordinating defensive positions all prove crucial, especially on harder difficulty levels where enemy numbers swell dramatically. The social element gives After The Fall much of its longevity—playing with friends or an active online group transforms otherwise straightforward missions into dynamic, unpredictable encounters. Communication, even minimal, adds a sense of camaraderie that fits naturally with the desperate fight for survival. The hub area, where players meet between runs, reinforces the feeling of a small but determined survivor community carving out life in frozen ruins.

Progression is anchored by collectible floppy disks that unlock new weapon modifications, items, and upgrades. This system encourages repeated play, nudging you to refine your loadout and experiment with different weapon builds. While simple, it provides a steady reward loop that complements the game’s run-centric structure. Each completed mission brings new resources, pushing you to take on tougher routes, face more aggressive Snowbreed variants, and continuously improve your arsenal. Over time, the challenge ramps up in a satisfying way, making early missions feel dramatically different once you’re better equipped and more experienced.

The game does, however, show the limitations of its scope. Content variety is one of the main criticisms—mission layouts follow a similar pattern, enemy types are somewhat limited, and the absence of a strong narrative means the world’s backstory remains mostly implied rather than explored. While the moment-to-moment combat is engaging, players looking for a story-driven VR campaign or a vast sandbox may find the structure too repetitive. Technical issues, such as occasional matchmaking hiccups or minor graphical glitches, can also interrupt an otherwise fluid experience. Yet even with these limitations, the core loop remains enjoyable because it leans so heavily on atmosphere, gunplay, and the energy of cooperative action.

In the end, After The Fall succeeds by focusing on what VR does best: immersion, physical engagement, and shared adrenaline. It offers a polished cooperative shooter experience wrapped in a striking frozen-apocalypse aesthetic, delivering a steady stream of intense firefights and memorable co-op moments. While it may not offer deep narrative layers or expansive mission variety, it compensates with tight combat mechanics, strong social features, and the satisfying grind of upgrading weapons and tackling harder routes. For VR players seeking a reliable, action-packed co-op game with a distinctive atmosphere, it stands as one of the more memorable entries in the genre.

After the Fall is one of those amazing games for the first `n` hours until you become acutely aware of all of its flaws. It is sad to see yet another VR game butchered - major problems that could be fixed with little effort.

* Major design issue - Snowies that crawl on the floor have collision and are obscured by tonnes of dead bodies. They can clip through them and hide within, blocking your own movement (even tho irl you'd probably easily step or jump over them) and attacking you without you knowing they even exist.

* Major design issue - Sound doesn't exist. A large boss (e.g. brute) can spawn behind you and hit you til you're dead without you knowing about it, there is absolutely no sound clue to anything, while you'd expect it to have proper stomping footsteps, the bashing he does should also have sound, all of it is silent. Instead you often get dead zombies colliding (glitching) with the environment causing massive ear-rape. Similarly some weapons have poor sound design (auto shotgun, amplified by poorly implemented chip = bug/exploit)

* Major implementation issue - Avatar scale. It's a multiplayer VR game, you've gotta have properly scaled and positioned avatars. Why is the viewport about 15cm above the head? Why are all the avatars kneeling and if you move your head up they scale up to keep their feet on the floor and head... 15cm under the viewport? Why is it using the worst inverse kinematics I've ever seen? There are decent IKs on the market, why not use them...

* Major implementation issue - Female avatars are in fact male avatars with absolutely no chest to speak of, the only difference between them is slightly wider hips. But even that might be just my impression given by perhaps different pose in the thumbnail. They are in fact male bodies. I'm greatly disappoint by this in this day and age when most game developers generate at least some effort for equality. I'd rather have a few less avatars of a better quality than this disaster.

* Implementation issue - Hoard mode is impossible without a full group - it doesn't scale with the number of players and there is no AI to help.

* Implementation issue - Pump shotgun in VR doesn't work, why are you trying to do it? Half the time the whole pumping thing doesn't actually load the next bullet for some reason. This inconsistent behaviour costs lives - either you die to it several times a run, or you pump 2x for every bullet to increase the chances of success. Still gonna probably die to not being able to shoot when it doesn't pump a fresh bullet for a fresh zombo 2x in a row.

* Design issue - Seems that it's customary in VR shooters to have a gameplay mechanic aimed towards some weapon drawback to balance out some positive properties... Recoil. Do you know what happens when you have a real life gun stock? Many PCVR fans do. Well the immersion goes out the window when you have to point your automatic rifle into the floor to shoot straight ahead, hunched over like a gremlin and hurting your neck looking up to see where you're shooting. Love it. I'd rather have 50% less damage and have recoil limits that don't get me into such dumb position. It's VR, not pancake, VR is about virtual REALITY. Maybe in the 3rd installment of this zombo game we will get a bit closer to the R of that equation and not point at the floor while shooting straight <3

So After The Fall is another vr game made by Vertigo Games, their other popular game Arizona Sunshine zombie game was really fun. That set the bar for their vr game to like that & better but with After The Fall it kinda fall flat. For $39.99 you expect to get good quality graphics, decent optimization & good content. Optimization is bad, the game keeps phasing in & out during game play quit a lot & the content is well lacking. Four or five maps, 6 weapons, 3 mini bosses & 1 super boss but its just a re-skin of one of the mini bosses just scaled bigger.

The deluxe edition for same price as launch version ($9.99 upgrade) you get access to an additional farming run, an additional pvp arena, additional game mode, additional weapon & exclusive character skin. After downloading the deluxe edition I saw no difference in content from the launch version & deluxe version. Same maps, weapons  & character skin. I don't know why you have a deluxe edition for content that is that same as launch version.

I feel that this was made for Oculus in-mind more & they imported it over to steam without really testing it. Here are issues I found in both steam & Oculus
1. Magazines will randomly drop out of my hand
2. Ammo pouch can't be moved in different area
3. Training doesn't give you full training
4. Settings doesn't let you full customize to your liking  at start up, have to manually go & do it
5. Manual reloading with off hand is jank, doesn't fully track reloading

These may seem small stuff but to some this is important to their gameplay experience. So with that After The Fall gets 4/10 making it under average. Maybe with more updates, more content & better optimization this game could be a better & not so cold to play. I would not recommend buying After The Fall but instead recommend buying Vertigo Games zombie game Arizona Sunshine.

TLDR; The game is mediocre. Arizona and its DLCs were much better, quality wise. 

In Arizona the zombies felt like a threat and you felt like you a had purpose. Here the zombies (that look more like snow aliens with giant heads) are uninspired and are just cannon fodder, they are only a threat due to their numbers. The gameplay is not satisfying, you don't get any sense of achievement. You're just glad when the wave is over and can move to the next location where you'll just repeat the whole process, grinding your way through the waves of uninspired levels and enemies. 
It's pretty much the opposite of what Arizona was. Arizona had depth and charm due to its story, level design and sense of danger created by the enemies. The Devs should have improved on what made the first game a hit, expanding the story, the levels, weapon and enemy variation. This is just a bad L4D ripoff with zero innovation or interesting features. I'm not even addressing the grind required for the unlocks. The only good feature to me is the localized damage on the zombies, which is well done, but it's not nearly enough to compensate all the other flaws. 
If you want to shoot zombies solo or coop, you're much better of playing Arizona Sunshine, it's a much superior game at every level.

Edit: Just to make my point, after playing half an hour of Arizona, I stopped to buy all the DLCs, because I could already tell that the game was a lot of fun and that the devs succeeded at creating a really good zombie shooter. Playing After the fall, I couldn't even force myself to finish the first level as I was already bored after the second wave of enemies.  It's also important to note that it's not nostalgia, as I am a fairly new VR player.

-manual reload is not ideal on touch controllers. I'm surprised they released the game with manual reload feeling like an afterthought. -It's a game with an arcade like feel, nothing wrong with that. So when I finally can get my magazine into my starter handgun, snap the magazine in when it gets about half way. -doors are a pain, half of them you can just walk through without even opening all the way, your AI people just walk through them, the zombies just walk through. It's just a visual bug and can easily be addressed, but again, how does that make it past launch?
-there's no way to say which hand is your primary hand, I say that because this game is adamant about snapping everything to my left hand. I'm trying to reload my starter pistol in my right hand. NOPE. swap to left. I do the exact same gesture but mirrored (reload gun in left hand with right) and it pulls the chamber back every time. 
-I pick up new guns in my right hand it won't let me assign them to right slot, only the left. It won't let me drop the gun in the right slot either as if it's already assigned.
-I collected two floppy discs on the first mission. Put one in an arcade machine at a checkpoint. Window pops up that your disc was saved. The arcade won't let me put in another disc. Overall, if at a sale price, this title is easier to swallow.  They have improved a few things and added a bit of content since launch, but there's still plenty of shortfalls here.  Regardless, friends and I that picked up this game on sale have found hours of co-op enjoyment recently.

Lukewarm recommendation if you're looking for a simplistic, arcade shooter with multiplayer if on sale.

I'm leaving the negative review status, though, because the devs could still make some simple fixes to make this VR title more on par with other recent ones in the quality of life department:

-This game really needs a calibration setting for aimpoint -- try aiming in-game and extending your index finger like you're pointing at an object -- this is your natural aimpoint that real pistol grips are angled for; you may notice the in-game weapon aim not matching the natural aimpoint.  Most VR shooters have a calibration setting to change this to account for different controllers/hands.  This title does not have this, and it severely affects quick aim, especially noticeable with holo/reflex sights on pistols.

 -Pistol belt/ammo rig really needs better calibration settings;  as is, the ammo pouches are  far too high on the torso and the pistol holsters cannot lower to drop-leg height on me; the calibration seems to have a floor that needs to be extended to allow for this lower/more realistic setup.

-There's something very tedious about the magazine insertion to the weapons using manual reloading.  A motion that should load the mag can sometimes get stuck outside the mag well and not load.  Other VR shooters have much smoother mechanics that feel more natural for reloading.

-Sentiment still remains that there should be more content for the normal price point.

-Not a quick fix, but this title would benefit from cursory backup melee options, a rifle/long gun sling position on the back/shoulder instead of those occupying pistol holster slots, more weapon storage space, and more character skins.

Some positive changes they've made:

-They have added a bit more content -- not enough, but there's more game modes now.

-There's a mechanism for changing character appearance now.

-The manual reloading mechanic now adds damage instead of rewards, which helps offset effectiveness vs arcade reloading users.
